**Name a class for what it does, and the file for the class.** The name says the idea, and ends in the suffix its kind uses — `*Plugin`, `*Dependency`, `*RuntimeModule`, `*Warning`, `*Error`, `*Module`, `*Factory`, `*Generator`, `*Parser`, `*Template` (546 of 668 PascalCase files in `lib/`). A file exporting one class takes that name; where the two disagree, rename whichever is wrong — often the file. Exempt: core nouns (`Compiler`, `Chunk`), helper and data-structure modules, and any module exporting several things.

-**A name never** invents a role suffix (`lib/` has no `*Controller`, `*Manager`, `*Service` or `*Util` — a class that controls a thing is the thing), carries a `Webpack` prefix where the bare word is free, or repeats another class in `lib/`, since a stack trace and `types.d.ts` show the name alone.

+**A name never** invents a role suffix (`lib/` has no `*Controller`, `*Manager`, `*Service` or `*Util` — a class that controls a thing is the thing), carries a `Webpack` prefix where the bare word is free, or repeats another class in `lib/`, since a stack trace and `types.d.ts` show the name alone. The one exception is a language's syntax layer (`lib/{css,html,javascript}/syntax*.js`), where the namespace names the language: it declares `Tokenizer`, `SyntaxParser` or `SyntaxPath`, not `CssTokenizer`, and exports its `SyntaxParser` as `Parser`. `types.d.ts` publishes a class whose name another directory also declares as `<Directory><Name>` (`CssTokenizer`), exported under the bare name in its namespace; `yarn lint:class-names` fails a repeat two directories cannot tell apart, or whose qualified name another class holds.

Checks for `eval` first scan the tree's identifier names once. Trees without that name skip function-body searches; others cache each search result. Both caches reset between prints because node numbers are reused.

- `syntax.js` reaches `parser` and `printer` through getters: parsing never loads the printer, and the printer loads the parser to read an asset into a `SyntaxTree`. It is the only parser: a source it refuses is refused, and terser's parse options for what is not a program (`parse.expression`, `parse.strict`, `parse.experimental_typescript`) are refused too. `toEstreeObject(node, options?)` builds the ESTree object of a node of the last parse (`SyntaxTree#estreeObject` of any tree), the same object for the same options: `ecmaVersion` (the edition whose fields it holds, the parse's by default), `ranges`, `locations` and `sourceFile`, as acorn's options of those names. A node spanning at most 1024 characters comes with its whole subtree built at once, as plain data properties; a longer one holds each child as an own accessor that reads it from the tree the first time it is read, so a long subtree nothing reads has no objects; the next parse copies the columns the objects made so far read. It bridges hooks and plugins while the parser moves to that struct-of-arrays tree. A reader the next parse must not disturb takes the tree with `takeParsedTree()` and releases it once read. The tree already reads as [the node path](#the-node-path) does, a node passed last: `type`, `start`, `end`, `range`, `name`, `value`, `field`, `fieldCount`, `flag` and `textOf` with the `NodeType`, `Field`, `Flag` and `Part` that `syntax.parser` exports. `SourceProcessor` walks the tree a parse writes as the CSS and HTML ones walk theirs, each visitor handed that path and the children taken in source order (a template's quasis and expressions in turn). Asked for `mode: "minify"`, the same walk prints: `syntax-printer.js`'s `printer` returns each node's text from its children's, as `minify` prints a source it neither compresses nor mangles, comments left out and terser's format options read from `format`. A minify walks the tree its own parse wrote (`walkSyntaxTree`) with the comments it keeps, a name printed inside its parent's text where none of its own is read: each is taken as terser's printer reaches it, by the node holding its token, and printed once the text before it is, which a text opening with it leaves to the node printing that text. What terser's stream reads off the text before a node — `has_parens` before a function or object starting a statement, `!--`, `</script` — it reads off the tree instead, the one `parsedTree()` returns while the walk runs, and through `ancestor(level)`, a node enclosing the current one; and each child's text is read once (`PrintContext#consume`), so a long one is made flat and its pieces let go as it is printed.
-- `syntax-tokenizer.js` — the tokenizer, acorn's `tokenize.js` and `tokencontext.js`, as `JavascriptTokenizer`, which `SyntaxParser` extends.
+- `syntax-tokenizer.js` — the tokenizer, acorn's `tokenize.js` and `tokencontext.js`, as `Tokenizer`, which `SyntaxParser` extends.

- `syntax-parser.js` — the acorn-derived core and every production in one file (any parse reaches the productions). `parseProgram(input, pos, options)` is the one entry, a build's included: it writes a new `SyntaxTree`, read through `A`, and returns the program's node. `toEstreeObject` builds a node's ESTree object from the tree, leaving out the fields acorn's objects lack at the parse's edition. Beside `sourceType` (and `auto`, a module turning into a script at a top-level `return`), `ecmaVersion` and `parseError`, it takes acorn's grammar and token options, `comments` (an array to collect into) and `importPhases`. `JavascriptParser`, the concatenation, the minifier, the `SourceProcessor` and the tooling all parse through it; only a custom `parse` function replaces it. The tree path writes each node into the tree, or the one a caller passes as `syntaxTree`, as it finishes, children before their parent, an id in the tree's columns rather than an object; a key, a module name and an exported declaration are written as they are read and the checks read their names back by node, a modifier read as a key first (`get`, `set`, `async`) taken back off the tree; a function before its body ends stays an object until it is written, and an expression read as a pattern after all is retyped in place. Every edition takes a tree, each owned production checking the edition where acorn does; parser plugins do not, since acorn's own productions read their nodes back. A parse into ESTree objects keeps acorn's productions for an older edition, whose objects lack the newer fields. `regexp.js` (pattern validator) is the one on-demand piece: `parseProgram`'s `WebpackParser` reaches it for every regexp literal below `ecmaVersion` 16 and, from 16 on, only for a pattern the host engine rejected; the exported `Parser` reaches it for every regexp literal. Never `require` it from a build path.

- **Scopes:** `syntax.scopes` (`webpack.javascript.syntax.scopes`) is `ScopeAnalyzer.js`'s analysis, loaded on first use. A parse with `scopes: true`, or a `ScopeLog` it empties and refills, records names and scopes as it goes, and `analyzeScope(program)` builds the scope tree from that log in one pass. A tree with no log, such as one `fromEstreeObject` wrote, is walked instead. Call it before the next parse: it reads the tree `A` reads. Concatenation reuses one log through `JavascriptParser._parseScopes`, so a build without `optimization.concatenateModules` or `optimization.avoidEntryIife` never records.
